pr_body:
If a pointer is accessed via reflection it is boxed into a
`System.Reflection.Pointer`. This type didn't override `Equals` and
`GetHashCode`, meaning instances are equal by reference.

On the other hand, pointers are compared by their value. Since
value types are equal by either memcmp or memberwise equality
(via reflection), the outcome of an equality test of a pointer itself
depends on the type that holds that pointer.

Fix #42457
pr_comments: These changes need to be added to the [System.Runtime reference assembly](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/src/libraries/System.Runtime/ref/System.Runtime.cs#L8552-L8559). Presumably, this means that they also need to go through the [API review process](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/docs/project/api-review-process.md).

Thanks @reflectronic! You're right in that these new overrides should be reflected in the reference assembly. But this shouldn't require formal API review since we're not introducing new API; we're only overriding existing API. From the review perspective this is considered no change.

issue_context.title: Behavior for pointer equality depends on its declaring struct.
comments: Relying on default ValueType.Equals is probably always a bad idea but this looks like a bug 🤔

review_comments:
There are no negative test cases present; e.g., `Assert.False(Pointer.Box((void*)0x12341234, typeof(int*)).Equals(Pointer.Box((void*)0x12341230, typeof(int*)))`.

There should also be positive tests for hash code equality. These can be rolled in to the newly introduced `*_AreEqual` tests if you want. I'm not too worried about negative tests for `GetHashCode`.

Is comparison of the pointer Type intentionally omitted here?

Either way, this case should be covered by the tests.
I knew I've forgotten something. There is no way to get pointers to polymorphic types in .net right? So type hierarchy isn't an issue here?

There might be some scenarios for wanting to ignore the type. For instance:

```cs
int* pA = 0x12340000;
uint* pB = (uint*)pA;
Console.WriteLine(pA == pB); // prints 'True'
Console.WriteLine(Pointer.Box(pA, typeof(int)).Equals(Pointer.Box(pB, typeof(uint))); // prints ???
Console.WriteLine(Pointer.Box(pA, typeof(int)) == Pointer.Box(pB, typeof(uint)); // prints ???
```

As an aside, an immutable sealed class that logically represents a standalone value and which has overridden `Equals` should probably also override `operator ==`.

Hmm interesting, .net is different to C++ in that regard. C++ doesn't allow comparison of different pointer types. Good to know.

So it looks like .net doesn't differentiate between pointer types when it comes to equality, i.e. `short*` and `double*` are also compared solely by their address.

> There might be some scenarios for wanting to ignore the type.

You can handle all these scenarios today, by unboxing the Pointer using Pointer.Unbox and comparing what you need yourself. 

The behavior change for Equals is convenience, it is not enabling any fundamentally new capability. We can argue which one is the most convenient behavior to make it the default.

> .net is different to C++ in that regard. 

More precisely, C# is different to C++ here.  And C is different from C++ and it does allow comparison of different pointer types. All C#, C and C++ can run on .NET today.

> The behavior change for Equals is convenience

And as with every behavior change, it is also a potential breaking change.

> and it does allow comparison of different pointer types

well standard C++ [doesn't allow](https://godbolt.org/z/Kb5P83) this, except for objects within the same type hierarchy.

> The behavior change for Equals is convenience

I'd argue that `a.Equals(a)` evaluating to `false` is a bug.

I've only added tests now and left the implementation as is. I didn't add type checking because the unboxed pointers aren't type checked either. `operator==` wasn't added because it is not required to fix `a.Equals(a)`.

As I said above 

> I didn't add type checking because the unboxed pointers aren't type checked either

I could add type checking if you think that this is the better approach. It doesn't affect the bug fix.

I don't think the type check is necessary, since treating a pointer like an "untyped" address should be sufficient and may be desired in some cases.

However, please add a test that asserts the behavior like the `DifferentPointerTypes_Null_AreEqual` I added above.
